shortlist.title: Ring cameras go mobile as Amazon debuts AI-powered security drone and robot
shortlist.summary: Amazon's roaming Ring Robotics devices will debut in late 2026 and early 2027.
shortlist.raw_text: Amazon is betting that many Ring customers will also want an AI-powered security drone and robot patrolling their homes or offices. But the company’s upcoming Ring Robotic products are also certain to intensify privacy concerns previously raised around a prior Amazon attempt to popularize a flying security camera. The Ring Rover Cam and Ring Drone Cam are expected to reach customers starting at the end of 2026 and in early 2027, respectively, according to an Amazon announcement posted on November 10. Amazon describes the devices as relying on an AI Pilot system that uses each device’s cameras along with “specialized vision models, on-device sensors and cloud processing” to plan patrol routes while autonomously navigating around obstacles such as furniture. Both devices also use that AI Pilot system to digitally map the floor plan of the customer’s home or business. This setup process occurs after the customer carries the Ring drone through their indoor spaces or allows the Ring Rover to do some autonomous exploration. Read full article Comments

shortlist.raw_text: Tactile sensing is an indispensable modality for contact-rich dexterous manipulation, a capability that hints at the ultimate frontiers of embodied intelligence. However, commercially available tactile sensors are still at a relatively early stage of development, with each type of sensor offering irreplaceable strengths alongside its own drawbacks. A key challenge is thus to free tactile understanding from sensor-specific physics, so that embodied models can effectively leverage heterogeneous tactile data. To this end, we develop LingBot-Touch, a tactile foundation model characterized by the following properties. (i) Our model yields a unified representation across different tactile sensors (i.e., piezoresistive, magnetic, and visuotactile sensors), and is easily extensible to new sensor types. (ii) The resulting tactile tokens are plug-and-play: they can be seamlessly integrated into policy models across paradigms, from diffusion policy to vision-language-action (VLA) models such as π_{0.5} and LingBot-VLA, consistently enhancing manipulation dexterity. (iii) Extensive experiments, spanning simulation and real-robot deployments across multiple hardware platforms, demonstrate that our tactile representation substantially benefits complex manipulation tasks while maintaining strong computational efficiency. We believe the findings in this work demonstrate the potential of leveraging cross-sensor data to scale tactile learning, and offer encouraging insights for the design of future hardware and embodied models.

shortlist.raw_text: External memory enables LLM agents to improve from experience by distilling trajectories of past tasks into concise lessons for new tasks. However, memory can also lead to memory-induced degradation, where an agent fails on tasks it would solve without memory, often because it follows a lesson that is incorrect, or misapplies or misreads a valid one. This is because lessons are inferred from trajectories labeled only with task success or failure, yet are typically provided without the trajectories they came from, leaving the agent no way to check them. To address this, we introduce WikiTrace, an evidence-linked memory system designed to let agents check each lesson against its original trajectory. Specifically, motivated by the finding that a trajectory often still holds the evidence needed to catch an erroneous lesson, WikiTrace stores each lesson as a concise insight linked to a summary of why its trajectory succeeded or failed and to the raw trajectory itself. Then, on a new task, the agent starts from all insights and, whenever one lacks details needed to act, conflicts with another, or comes from a failed task, descends through its links with terminal tools to fill in missing details or correct the insight before acting. We validate WikiTrace on five agentic benchmarks, showing that it consistently outperforms existing memory approaches and a baseline given the same insights alone, while also reducing memory-induced degradation. Our code is available at https://github.com/yukyeongleee/wikitrace

Title: Gilbert + Tobin rethinks the business of law with AI

Text:
A conversation with Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer at Gilbert + Tobin.

Research notes on: Australian law firm Gilbert + Tobin transforms its legal practice and business model through AI adoption led by CEO Sam Nickless.
(Found by web search. Some coverage may be older background. Use it for context and explanation, but don't present older events as new, and keep the main story's facts primary.)

Coverage from Law: "ELTEMATE CEO: Legal Departments ‘Leading the Way’ With AI Adoption"
The 2026 Legalweek Leaders in Tech Law Awards honor those who have made significant contributions to legal innovation from law firms, corporate legal departments and legal tech providers. These awards ...

Background (Legal technology, Wikipedia):
Legal technology, also known as legal tech, refers to the use of technology and software to provide legal services and support the legal industry. Legal technology encompasses the use of traditional software architecture and web technologies, such as searchable databases of case law and other legal authority, as well as machine learning technologies, such as those used to automatically search documents for purposes of due diligence or discovery. Work on making contracts more easy to use involve aspects of user experience design, and artificial intelligence.

Background (Enterprise legal management, Wikipedia):
Enterprise legal management (ELM) is a practice management strategy of corporate legal departments, insurance claims departments, and government legal and contract management departments.
text:
An Australian law firm is using AI to overhaul its business model.

CEO Sam Nickless is pushing changes far beyond basic document automation.

The billing structure is the real target.

Traditional legal technology focused on narrow administrative tasks, like searching case law databases or running due diligence.

Law firms sell time.

When software completes hours of research in minutes, selling time stops working.

Gilbert + Tobin is trying to adapt before the market forces them to.

Led by Nickless, the firm is tying AI adoption directly to how it structures its business and serves clients.

Standard legal tech covers specific functions:
• Searchable databases for case law and legal authority
• Machine learning to search documents during due diligence
• Design improvements to make contracts easier to read

Speed alone creates a structural trap.

If software cuts five hours of effort down to five minutes, hourly billing reduces revenue proportionally.

My read: legal AI won't just speed up lawyers, it will dismantle the billable hour.

The limitation is real. This is an early strategic transition, and the firm has not publicly detailed its new revenue metrics.

If software handles the bulk of your output, how will you charge for your work?

Source: OpenAI, with reporting from Law
alt_openings:
Corrective
Line 1: Selling billable hours stops making sense the moment AI enters a law firm.
Line 2: Gilbert + Tobin CEO Sam Nickless is restructuring his practice around that reality.
When to prefer: Best when targeting founders, partners, and consultants who personally bill by the hour and feel the immediate commercial threat.

Tool as subject
Line 1: AI is forcing Australian law firm Gilbert + Tobin to alter its business model.
Line 2: CEO Sam Nickless is reorganizing how the firm captures value from legal work.
When to prefer: Best for general corporate audiences who want a direct, objective news hook about corporate strategy.

Your X
Line 1: Your lawyer's billable hour is on the verge of collapsing.
Line 2: Executive leadership at Gilbert + Tobin is already changing how they charge clients.
When to prefer: Best when writing for buyers of legal services, like corporate managers and finance leaders who pay external legal bills.

Pick: The Corrective opening. It directly names the fundamental business conflict (billable hours vs. AI efficiency) immediately, giving smart professionals a strong thesis to click "see more" and test against their own business models.
headline: How AI is dismantling the legal billable hour
